Chapter Four: Cultural Adaptation and Everyday Misunderstandings
Let’s take a closer look at what it really means to adjust to life in North Korea. It's not just about picking up a new language or following unfamiliar customs. It’s about learning to see the world through a lens shaped by years of isolation, shared struggles, and a collective spirit. If you’re an outsider, this journey can leave you feeling lost at times, maybe even frustrated—but it’s always eye-opening.
The very first hurdle? Communication. Even with a translator by your side, things can get muddled. You ask for a meeting and it might sound like a demand. Offer a suggestion and it could be taken as criticism. Before long, you realize—words aren’t everything. What matters just as much is your intent, and the way you listen.
Imagine this: One day, a foreign manager steps onto the factory floor, ready to introduce a new workflow. The plan’s simple—just rearrange the assembly line to boost efficiency. But the workers hesitate, unsure whether they’re even allowed to change things. That’s when a supervisor quietly pulls the manager aside and explains—here, in North Korea, innovation isn’t always welcomed. Folks are taught to stick to the rules, and trying something new can feel risky.
So, the manager changes tactics. He rolls up his sleeves and works side by side with the team. Slowly, the workers begin to open up, offering small suggestions and tweaks—little changes that end up making a big difference. It’s not fast, but it builds trust and shows everyone that even in a rigid system, change is possible.
Now, let’s talk about social customs. In meetings, hierarchy is everything. The most senior person always speaks first, and everyone else waits patiently. You almost never hear open disagreement, and criticism—if it happens at all—comes wrapped in kindness. For someone used to lively debates, this might seem confusing. But after a while, it starts to make sense. Here, harmony matters more than confrontation, and relationships are built slowly, on a foundation of respect.
These differences show up outside work, too. Take dinner invitations—they’re both an honor and a subtle test. If you’re invited, you’re expected to try every dish, join in the toasts in just the right order, and pay attention to every little gesture. Even a simple mistake, like refusing food, can accidentally cause offense.
Picture this: one evening, a foreign guest sits at a colleague’s table for a family celebration. The meal is impressive, crafted from ingredients that aren’t easy to find. The host beams with pride, eager to share his culture and stories. As the evening unfolds, laughter fills the room, and for a moment, all those cultural barriers just melt away. What’s left is a sense of shared humanity.
But let’s be honest—misunderstandings still happen. Maybe a joke doesn’t land, a gesture is misinterpreted, or a helpful suggestion backfires. Each little misstep becomes a lesson in humility, reminding you that adapting is something both sides have to work at.
Over time, though, things get easier. You start to pick up on the unspoken cues, you know when to speak up and when it’s better to just listen. Friendships grow deeper, and that early awkwardness slowly fades. What you end up learning isn’t just about customs or language—it’s about patience, about empathy, and about seeing life through someone else’s eyes.
Living in North Korea means adapting every single day. The rules are different, the expectations unfamiliar, but the rewards are real. If you’re open to learning, the journey will give you more than just new skills. It offers a richer understanding of what it means to be human, shaped by history, hardship, and—most importantly—hope.
